intro: A sprig of mint brings a spoiled jar of air back to life. A slice of cucumber weeps when you salt it. A cut heals in a week and a bruise fades. A tree that weighs more than a car was built from gas. These are not separate mysteries. Each one is a cell doing chemistry: taking things in through a membrane thinner than anything humans can make, building and breaking molecules, capturing energy and spending it, and, when the time is right, becoming two.

This unit starts with water and carbon and works up. You will see what the four families of molecules are made of and how enzymes make reactions run. You will look inside a cell the way Hooke and Leeuwenhoek first did, and learn what the microscope on this site can and cannot show. You will trace a carbon atom from the air over an Illinois cornfield into a leaf, into sugar, into a muscle, and back into the air as you breathe out.

By the end you will be able to explain why cells are small, how a plant grows from air, why you need oxygen, what a cancer cell has broken, and how one cell became the trillions that are reading this sentence. Along the way you will see how each of these ideas was argued over, tested and sometimes gotten wrong before it was gotten right.
bigQuestion: How does a cell turn air, water and sunlight into a living, growing body?

timeline.t: Van Helmont's willow experiment is published: a tree gains 164 pounds while the soil loses two ounces.
Robert Hooke looks at cork through his microscope and names the tiny boxes cells.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek sees living single-celled organisms swimming in drops of water.
Joseph Priestley reports that a sprig of mint restores air in which a candle has burned out.
Jan Ingenhousz shows plants restore air only in light and only with their green parts.
Schleiden and Schwann argue that all plants and all animals are made of cells.
Rudolf Virchow states that every cell comes from a cell that already existed.
Walther Flemming describes the stages of mitosis in stained salamander cells.
James Sumner crystallizes urease and shows that an enzyme is a protein.
Hans Krebs works out the cycle inside mitochondria that strips carbon from food.
Melvin Calvin uses radioactive carbon to trace how plants build sugar from carbon dioxide.
Shinya Yamanaka turns adult skin cells back into pluripotent stem cells with four genes.

words.d: having a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, like a water molecule
a very large molecule built from many smaller repeating units, such as a protein or starch
a protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction without being used up
a small structure inside a eukaryotic cell that does a specialized job
letting some substances pass through a membrane while blocking others
the diffusion of water across a membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles
keeping conditions inside a cell or body steady while the outside changes
the process in which plants use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water
the process in which cells break down glucose using oxygen to make ATP
the molecule cells use to carry energy in small, spendable amounts
the division of a nucleus into two nuclei with identical sets of chromosomes
the process by which a cell becomes a specialized type by switching genes on and off

test.q: Which property of water makes it such a good solvent for the molecules cells use?
choices: Its molecules are polar, with charged ends that pull apart other polar or charged substances
It is a gas at body temperature
It has a very low boiling point
test.why: Water's charged ends surround ions and polar molecules and pull them into solution.

test.q: Which macromolecule is a chain of amino acids folded into a working shape?
test.why: Proteins are amino acid chains whose folded shape sets their job. DNA is a nucleic acid; starch is a carbohydrate.

test.q: Why does raising temperature far above normal stop an enzyme from working?
choices: The enzyme runs out of substrate
The enzyme turns into a carbohydrate
Heat changes the enzyme's shape so its active site no longer fits its substrate
test.why: An enzyme is a protein. Too much heat unfolds it, and a misshapen active site cannot hold the substrate.

test.q: Why do cells stay small instead of growing very large?
choices: As a cell grows, its volume rises faster than its surface, and the surface cannot supply the inside
test.why: The surface-to-volume ratio falls as size increases. A large cell's center would be too far from any surface to be fed.

test.q: A cell seen under the microscope has no nucleus and a single loop of DNA. It is:
test.why: Lacking a nucleus is the defining trait of prokaryotes. Plants, animals and fungi are all eukaryotes.

test.q: Which best describes the structure of the cell membrane?
choices: A double layer of phospholipids with proteins embedded in it
test.why: The bilayer, with oily tails inside and polar heads outside, is studded with proteins that act as channels, pumps and receptors.

test.q: Potato slices are placed in salt water and shrink. What moved, and in which direction?
choices: Salt moved into the potato cells
Starch moved out of the cells
Water moved out of the potato cells toward the saltier solution by osmosis
test.why: Water diffuses across the membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles, so the cells lose water and shrink.

test.q: The sodium-potassium pump moves ions against their concentration gradients. What does this require?
test.why: Moving substances uphill is active transport, and it is paid for with ATP.

test.q: Blood sugar rises after a meal, insulin is released, and blood sugar falls. This is an example of:
test.why: The response, insulin, reverses the change and returns glucose toward its set point.

test.q: What did van Helmont's willow tree experiment show?
choices: Trees are made mainly of soil
A tree's added mass does not come from the soil
test.why: The tree gained 164 pounds while the soil lost about 2 ounces, ruling out soil as the source of mass.

test.q: In the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis, water is split. What happens to its parts?
choices: Both hydrogen and oxygen become part of glucose
The oxygen is released as gas and the hydrogen is used to make sugar
test.why: Splitting water replaces electrons chlorophyll loses. Oxygen gas is the by-product; hydrogen ends up in sugar.

test.q: Compared with fermentation, aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yields:
choices: Roughly fifteen times as much ATP
test.why: Fermentation yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis. The full aerobic route yields roughly 30.

test.q: Why is the Northern Hemisphere growing season visible in the Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record?
choices: Plants across the huge northern land areas take up carbon dioxide faster than it is released while they are leafed out
Hawaii gets more rain in summer
Cars are driven less in summer
test.why: Net photosynthesis over a whole hemisphere draws carbon dioxide down by a few parts per million each summer.

test.q: Which statement about mitosis is correct?
choices: It halves the number of chromosomes
It produces two cells genetically identical to the parent
It happens only in cancer cells
test.why: Mitosis copies and sorts identical chromosome sets. Meiosis, used to make sperm and eggs, halves and shuffles.

choices: A cell that has lost its DNA
A cell that can keep dividing and give rise to specialized cell types
A cell found only in plant stems
test.why: Stem cells have not finished differentiating. They renew themselves and produce specialized descendants.

write.prompt: A classmate claims that a plant gets its food from the soil, the way an animal gets food by eating. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning response that argues where a plant's mass and energy really come from, using at least two experiments or data sets from this unit.
tips: Claim: state clearly whether a plant's mass comes mostly from soil, water or air, and where its energy comes from.
Evidence: use van Helmont's willow numbers, Priestley's mint jar, Ingenhousz's light experiment, or the Mauna Loa seasonal dip.
Reasoning: connect each piece of evidence to the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis and to respiration.
The other side: explain what a plant really does get from soil, and why that does not make soil its food.
Use the words photosynthesis, carbon dioxide, glucose and ATP correctly at least once each.
